title: Strategy — Intermediate
summary: A networked RTS: formations, a supplies stock, fog that clients cannot write, medals, area of interest, transports, artillery budgets, and a save that recomputes vision.

sections.title: Formations and orders
sections.why: IA_Order calls ReceiveOrder only on Selected. Formation offsets stay data.
reading: Intermediate strategy orders still start at IA_Order. The excerpt branches if (Selected) and ProcessEvent on ReceiveOrder. A formation is not a tick that writes an offset on every member. The squad data names the shape. Each member reads its slot in that shape when it accepts the order. A vehicle in the formation is a member with a throttle, not a special case inside this branch.

The click that selects is a box trace once. Polling every unit against the mouse on Tick is the search the selection bool already replaced. An artillery order is still ReceiveOrder. The gun's fire mission is the unit's implementation, which then spends a shell. The order graph does not subtract shells, or every move would fire.

Fog must not flip because an order was issued into a hidden cell. The unit can be told to go. It cannot grant vision. Scoring hears the result if the order was an objective. A plain move does not award a medal. Netcode relevance, later, decides which of these units even exist on a client. The order still runs on the server for units the client cannot see.
Save stores the order id and the target, plus the formation id. It does not store every offset. Load must not replay IA_Order, or the formation steps twice.

The figure is the real Orders graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. IA_Order is the right click. It does not move every unit. Only the selected unit takes the order. Selection is a bool on the unit, not a search of the whole level. One interface. The tank and the infantry answer the same order. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 9 is `if (AActor* Target_tpl_orders_call = Cast<AActor>(nullptr)) { if (UFunction* Fn_tpl_orders_call = Target_tpl_o`.

Across this track, keep IA_Order, Selected, ReceiveOrder distinct. IA_Order calls ReceiveOrder only on Selected. Formation offsets stay data. if (Selected) calls ReceiveOrder. Save the formation id. Offsets are data. A move does not spend shells.

sections.title: The stock and the bill
sections.why: Spend subtracts a data cost on the authority. Artillery shells are a different budget.
reading: The stock is Supplies. Spend is the event. The excerpt assigns Supplies = (Supplies - 25.f) after an empty HasAuthority block. Nest it. Replace 25 with the data row for that building or that unit. A fire mission does not use this float. Shells are the artillery budget. Sharing the float makes a barrage bankrupt the base, or a barracks consume ammunition.

Scoring reads nothing here. A medal is not a refund. A refund is Spend with a negative cost from the same row, still on the authority. Income is a slow timer calling that path. Tick income runs through a pause and never checks that the refinery still exists.

The UI binds to the float. Replicating the icon is waste. Relevance does not change the stock: a player who cannot see the enemy still has a stock, because the stock is the player's, not a world actor in a cell. Orders call Spend only for purchases.
Save stores Supplies after the server write. Begin Play must not call Spend. A vehicle's fuel can be a second stock with the same pattern, not a reuse of Supplies, or driving drains the build money.

The figure is the real Economy graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. Spend is the order to build. It is not Tick. Only the authority changes supplies. Read the stock before you subtract. The data row should own this cost. Twenty five is the sample. Stock minus cost. Write the new stock. Replicate the number, not the icon. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 7 is `if (HasAuthority()) { /* authority */ } // node:tpl_economy_auth`. Line 8 is `Supplies = (Supplies - 25.f); // node:tpl_economy_set`.

Across this track, keep Spend, Supplies, Has Authority distinct. Spend subtracts a data cost on the authority. Artillery shells are a different budget. Supplies = (Supplies - 25.f) inside HasAuthority, cost from data. Shells are the artillery budget. Fuel is a third stock if the mode has vehicles.

assignment.model: Supplies = (Supplies - 25.f) inside HasAuthority, cost from data. Shells are the artillery budget. Fuel is a third stock if the mode has vehicles.

sections.title: Fog and the cheat
sections.why: Reveal at 0.25s sets Visible. Clients do not write it.
reading: Fog stays a vision pass. The excerpt starts Reveal every 0.25 seconds and assigns Visible = true on a hit. The sample still has no authority check. In a networked match that check is the anti-cheat: a client that writes Visible sees the enemy base. Nest a HasAuthority around the write before you ship the mode. The widget per spectator is not the replicated object. The bit is.

Orders into fog do not set the bit. Artillery that fires blind does not either, unless a spotter's trace is what Reveal already does. A barrage is not vision. Relevance is not vision either. A unit can be relevant to the server simulation and still invisible to a team. Do not collapse those two bools, or culling the actor deletes it from the other team's possible sight forever.

Hidden camps keep patrolling. The client skips the draw. Tick that walks every cell pays for cells where nothing moved. The 0.25 second pass is enough for a strategy map. Shortening it toward a frame is how the server falls over in a large match.
Save does not store Visible. After load, place units, then let Reveal run. A stored bit shows a ghost of where a truck was.

The figure is the real Fog of war graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. Begin Play starts the vision timer. Vision updates four times a second. Reveal is the vision pass. Line of sight from the unit. A clear trace marks the cell visible. True means this team can see the cell. Visible is replicated as a team fact, not per spectator widget. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 10 is `if (UWorld* World = GetWorld()) { FTimerHandle Timer_tpl_fog_timer; World->GetTimerManager().SetTimer(Timer_tp`. Line 15 is `FHitResult Hit_tpl_fog_trace; bool bHit_tpl_fog_trace = false; if (UWorld* World_tpl_fog_trace = GetWorld()) {`.

Across this track, keep Reveal, Visible, Authority distinct. Reveal at 0.25s sets Visible. Clients do not write it. Reveal runs at 0.25f and sets Visible = true. HasAuthority is the missing gate. Relevant is a different bool.

assignment.model: Reveal runs at 0.25f and sets Visible = true. HasAuthority is the missing gate. Relevant is a different bool.

sections.title: Medals and the board
sections.why: AwardMedal adds a data value on the authority. The board is local.
reading: Medals stay a server add. The excerpt assigns Score = (Score + 10.f) after an empty HasAuthority block. Nest it. The 10 is a sample. A kill, a capture, and a fire mission that hits a marked target can be different rows. A miss does not award. Fog revealing a unit does not award. Spending supplies does not award, and it must not share this float.

The board is a widget. It reads Score. Replicating the board actor, with its fonts and its rows, is the expensive version. Artillery's shell count is not the score. A successful mission may call AwardMedal after the impact, with the row's value. The impact itself is the gun's graph.

Vehicles destroyed call the same event. They do not add a literal in the throttle function, or every bump scores. Begin Play on load must not call AwardMedal. The stored score is the total. Calling the event again double-counts.
A client prediction of the number pops the board when the server add arrives. The widget can punch locally. The float waits.

The figure is the real Scoring graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. AwardMedal is the server event for a kill or an objective. Score changes on the authority. Current score. The data asset should own the medal value. Ten is the sample. Score plus the medal. Write score. The board reads it. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 7 is `if (HasAuthority()) { /* authority */ } // node:tpl_scoring_auth`. Line 8 is `Score = (Score + 10.f); // node:tpl_scoring_set`.

Across this track, keep AwardMedal, Score, Has Authority distinct. AwardMedal adds a data value on the authority. The board is local. Score = (Score + 10.f) inside HasAuthority in AwardMedal. The row owns the value. Throttle does not score.

assignment.model: Score = (Score + 10.f) inside HasAuthority in AwardMedal. The row owns the value. Throttle does not score.

sections.title: Relevance for a large map
sections.why: CheckAOI at 0.5s writes Relevant. It is not the fog bit.
reading: A strategy map has more units than an FPS has players. The excerpt starts CheckAOI at 0.5 seconds, looping, traces, and assigns Relevant = bHit after an empty HasAuthority block. Nest the write. This bool is who receives the actor. Fog's Visible is who on a team may see it. A unit can be relevant to the simulation host and invisible to the enemy. Collapsing them culls a unit the spotter was about to reveal.

The production system is the replication graph, with cells. The trace is the sample. Widgets, selection decals, and health bars are not replicated. The unit actor is, while Relevant. A truck can use a larger radius than a soldier. That radius is data. Ticking every wheel to decide relevance is the cost this timer removes.

Orders still execute on the server when the client does not have the actor. The client's first packet, when the unit becomes relevant, is a state: position, order id, supplies are not per unit. Artillery impacts the client cannot see still resolve on the server. Debris leaves relevance quickly.
Save does not store Relevant. After load the timer runs again from positions.

The figure is the real Area of interest graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. Begin Play starts the relevance timer. Relevance is checked twice a second, not every frame. CheckAOI is the relevancy pass. The server decides who is relevant. A stand-in for distance. A real AOI uses the replication graph. Relevant gates replication. The widget is not replicated. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 10 is `if (UWorld* World = GetWorld()) { FTimerHandle Timer_tpl_aoi_timer; World->GetTimerManager().SetTimer(Timer_tp`. Line 15 is `if (HasAuthority()) { /* authority */ } // node:tpl_aoi_auth`.

Across this track, keep CheckAOI, Relevant, Replication graph distinct. CheckAOI at 0.5s writes Relevant. It is not the fog bit. CheckAOI at 0.5f sets Relevant = bHit inside HasAuthority. Visible stays the team vision bit.

sections.title: Transports
sections.why: IA_Throttle writes Throttle on the authority. Orders can command the same vehicle.
reading: A transport is a unit the order system can command and a vehicle the driver can throttle. The excerpt assigns Throttle = IA_Throttle after an empty HasAuthority block. Nest it. ReceiveOrder on the same actor tells an AI driver where to go. The order does not write Throttle directly, or a formation click would stomp the driver's axis. The AI driver writes Throttle the way the input does, inside the authority.

On-foot speed, if any infantry graph exists, stays off this component. Wheels are local. Replicating each wheel so distant players see the suspension is the expensive version, and relevance should have dropped that truck before the wheels mattered. Fuel, if driving costs it, is its own stock, not Supplies and not Shells.

Fog draws the truck when Visible is true. Relevance decides whether the actor exists on the client at all. A truck can be heard by a larger radius. Artillery mounted on it uses the shell budget, not Throttle. Scoring hears a kill of the truck through AwardMedal, not through this assignment.
Save stores fuel and the current order. It rarely stores Throttle, which is a moment. Begin Play applies fuel before the simulation starts, or the truck lurches on an empty tank that has not loaded.

The figure is the real Vehicle drive graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. IA_Throttle is the axis. The chaos vehicle reads Throttle. The server owns the velocity. Write the axis. Do not replicate the wheel meshes. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 7 is `if (HasAuthority()) { /* authority */ } // node:tpl_vehicle-drive_auth`. Line 8 is `Throttle = IA_Throttle; // node:tpl_vehicle-drive_set`.

Across this track, keep IA_Throttle, Throttle, ReceiveOrder distinct. IA_Throttle writes Throttle on the authority. Orders can command the same vehicle. Throttle = IA_Throttle inside HasAuthority. The order calls ReceiveOrder. An AI driver then writes Throttle. Wheels stay local.

assignment.model: Throttle = IA_Throttle inside HasAuthority. The order calls ReceiveOrder. An AI driver then writes Throttle. Wheels stay local.

sections.title: Fire missions
sections.why: FireMission traces an impact and subtracts one shell on the authority.
reading: A fire mission is an order the gun implements. The excerpt's FireMission tests HasAuthority in an empty block, traces, and assigns Shells = (Shells - 1.f). Nest the subtract. The shell budget is the anti-spam. Without it a click streams impacts. The trace is the impact. Supplies are not decremented here. If a shell also costs money, the gun calls Spend with the row's cost as a second step. One float cannot be both budgets.

Blind fire does not set Visible. A spotter's Reveal is what lifts fog. Scoring runs only if the impact is a marked hit, through AwardMedal, not inside this subtract. A miss still spends the shell. That is the point of the budget.

The gun can be a vehicle. Throttle does not call FireMission. The order does. Relevance means a client who cannot see the gun still receives the impact if the impact is relevant, or not, by the impact's own radius. Spawning a shell actor per frame of flight replicates the arc. A delayed impact from the mission event is the cheap version.
Save stores Shells. Begin Play must not fire a mission because the gun had shells. Load the count. Do not spend one to prove the gun works.

The figure is the real Artillery graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. FireMission is the order. It is not a tick of the barrel. The server spawns the impact. The impact trace. Anti-spam lives in the shell count. Rounds left in the data asset budget. One shell. Budget minus one. Write the remaining shells. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 10 is `if (HasAuthority()) { /* authority */ } // node:tpl_artillery_auth`. Line 11 is `FHitResult Hit_tpl_artillery_trace; bool bHit_tpl_artillery_trace = false; if (UWorld* World_tpl_artillery_tra`.

Across this track, keep FireMission, Shells, Has Authority distinct. FireMission traces an impact and subtracts one shell on the authority. FireMission subtracts Shells by 1 inside HasAuthority. Supplies stay on Spend. Visible stays on Reveal.

assignment.prompt: A click streams impacts and also drains Supplies. What does the excerpt subtract, and what event should start the mission?
assignment.model: FireMission subtracts Shells by 1 inside HasAuthority. Supplies stay on Spend. Visible stays on Reveal.

sections.title: Save the battle
sections.why: Begin Play reads supplies, score, shells, fuel, and orders. Fog and relevance recompute.
reading: The battle slot packs Supplies, Score, Shells, fuel, formation ids, and the orders still running. It does not pack Visible or Relevant. The excerpt assigns SlotValue = 1.f at Begin Play and LoadSlot logs Loaded. Replace the stand-in with that struct. Begin Play must not call Spend, AwardMedal, or FireMission. Those would apply the battle a second time.

Tick saves a half-spent stock and a truck mid-bump. Write when the player asks, or on a slow match timer. Apply fuel before the vehicle simulates. Apply Shells before any gun can take an order. Start Reveal after units are placed. Start CheckAOI after positions exist. Starting vision first traces an empty map and then shows ghosts.

Offsets, wheel transforms, board widgets, and selection decals stay out. The formation id, the unit id, and the floats are enough. A destroyed building is an id in a list, the same way a destroyed wall was in the FPS slot. The mesh is the project's.
Two clients loading must read the server's struct. A client slot that spent locally is the desync the authority gate was meant to prevent, saved into a file.

The figure is the real Save / load slot graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. Begin Play writes the slot once. Do not write it from Tick. The member written into the payload. Make Struct builds the save payload. Keep the member on the component. Load is its own event. It does not run during the save. Break Struct reads one member. A print stands in for the load UI. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 8 is `FVector Made_tpl_saveload_make = FVector::ZeroVector; Made_tpl_saveload_make.X = 1.f; Made_tpl_saveload_make.Y`. Line 9 is `SlotValue = 1.f; // node:tpl_save-load_store`.

Across this track, keep Begin Play, SlotValue, Supplies distinct. Begin Play reads supplies, score, shells, fuel, and orders. Fog and relevance recompute. Reveal recomputes Visible. Begin Play must not call FireMission, Spend, or AwardMedal. Shells and Supplies are packed.

assignment.model: Reveal recomputes Visible. Begin Play must not call FireMission, Spend, or AwardMedal. Shells and Supplies are packed.
